title: Bidirectional BFS: Reykjavík’s Fastest Routes
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS shrink the search space by expanding from both the start and goal until the frontiers meet. This reel visualizes how graph-based street maps turn routing into an efficient shortest-path hunt.
ig_caption:
🚦 Reykjavík (Grandi) edition: Bidirectional BFS in action! 🌍✨

Bidirectional BFS runs **two simultaneous breadth-first searches**—one from the start node and one from the destination—on a street-map graph. When the two BFS frontiers **intersect**, you’ve found the shortest path in an unweighted graph, because BFS expands in layers of equal distance from each source. 🧠📍

In graph theory terms: we’re navigating a real-world network where intersections are vertices and road segments are edges. Compared to a single-source BFS, Bidirectional BFS typically cuts the explored area from **O(b^d)** down closer to **O(b^(d/2))**, making the visualization feel dramatically faster. ⚡️

Want me to overlay different road weights (turn costs / traffic) next? Comment “NEXT” and follow for more map-driven algorithm animations! 🔁💬
fb_caption:
🚗💡 Ever wondered how computers find routes on real street maps? This visualization uses **Bidirectional BFS**, a graph search method that explores outward from both the start and the goal at the same time. When the two search waves meet, you get the shortest path in an unweighted graph—often with far fewer explored intersections than standard BFS.

If you’re learning pathfinding, graph theory, or algorithm optimization, this is a great quick example of how reducing search space improves speed.
